Patients should take oral contraceptives at least one hour before administering exenatide due to its effect on slowing gastric emptying, which may reduce the absorption and efficacy of oral medications requiring rapid gastrointestinal absorption. Close monitoring is advised. 2. Ethinyl estradiol levels may be increased by fedratinib due to inhibition of hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 3. Fedratinib levels may be increased by ethinyl estradiol, potentially leading to enhanced effects. Avoid coadministration or consider alternative therapies. 4. Avoid coadministration of fedratinib, a CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 substrate, with dual inhibitors of these enzymes, as the interaction has not been studied. 5. Felbamate decreases ethinyl estradiol levels through an unknown mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 6. Fexinidazole increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP2E1 metabolism. Avoid coadministration or use alternative drugs, as fexinidazole also inhibits CYP3A4, increasing the risk of adverse effects. 7. Fezolinetant levels are increased by ethinyl estradiol due to inhibition of CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination is contraindicated, as weak, moderate, or strong CYP1A2 inhibitors can significantly increase fezolinetant plasma concentrations. 8. Finererone levels are increased by ethinyl estradiol through CYP3A4 inhibition. Monitor serum potassium levels during therapy initiation or dosage adjustments, and modify finererone dosage as needed. 9. Flibanserin levels may be increased by ethinyl estradiol due to CYP3A4 inhibition, potentially leading to increased adverse effects. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 10. Fluconazole increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 11. Fluvoxamine levels may be increased by ethinyl estradiol through CYP1A2 inhibition. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 12. Fosamprenavir coadministration with ethinyl estradiol may decrease amprenavir levels, potentially reducing virologic response. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may also be altered. Nonhormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 13. Fostemsavir increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting BCRP transporters. Avoid coadministration or adjust the dose of BCRP substrates. Ethinyl estradiol doses should not exceed 30 mcg/day. 14. Frovatriptan levels may be increased by ethinyl estradiol through CYP1A2 inhibition. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 15. Gemifloxacin decreases ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone and poses a low risk of contraceptive failure. 16. Grapefruit increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 17. Green tea levels may be increased by ethinyl estradiol due to decreased elimination. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 18. Griseofulvin decreases ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Nonhormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 19. Hemin effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 20. Heparin effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism, increasing the risk of thromboembolic disorders. This combination is contraindicated. 21. Hyaluronidase effects may be reduced by estrogens in large systemic doses, rendering tissues partially resistant to hyaluronidase action. Larger doses of hyaluronidase may be required for equivalent dispersing effects. 22. Idelalisib increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid coadministration or use alternative drugs, as idelalisib is a strong CYP3A inhibitor. 23. Iloperidone increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 24. Imipramine metabolism may be reduced by ethinyl estradiol, potentially increasing antidepressant serum concentrations and adverse effects. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 25. Indinavir coadministration with ethinyl estradiol may cause significant changes in estrogen plasma levels, potentially reducing hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Nonhormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 26. Insulin aspart effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 27. Insulin degludec effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 28. Inhaled insulin effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 32. Insulin lispro effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 33. Insulin NPH effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 34. Regular human insulin effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 35. Isavuconazonium sulfate increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid coadministration or use alternative drugs. 36. Istradefylline increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Consider dose reduction of sensitive CYP3A4 substrates. 37. Itraconazole increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 38. Ivosidenib decreases ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid coadministration or use alternative drugs. 39. Ketoconazole increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 40. Lamotrigine levels are decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to increased hepatic clearance, likely through induction of lamotrigine glucuronidation. Monitor closely. 41. Lapatinib levels may be increased by ethinyl estradiol through CYP3A4 inhibition. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 42. Larotrectinib increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 43. Lemborexant levels may be increased by ethinyl estradiol through CYP3A4 inhibition. Lower nightly doses of lemborexant are recommended. 44. Lenacapavir increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor closely for potential adverse reactions. 45. Leniolisib increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting BCRP transporters. Avoid coadministration or use alternative drugs. 46. Lesinurad decreases ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Nonhormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 47. Letrozole effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid coadministration with estrogens. 48. Levofloxacin decreases ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone and poses a low risk of contraceptive failure. 49. Levoketoconazole increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 50. Liraglutide effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 51. Lixisenatide decreases ethinyl estradiol levels by delaying gastric emptying, affecting absorption. Oral contraceptives should be taken at least one hour before or 11 hours after lixisenatide administration. 52. Lomitapide levels may be increased by ethinyl estradiol through CYP3A4 inhibition. Lomitapide doses should not exceed 30 mg/day. 53. Lonafarnib levels may be increased by ethinyl estradiol through CYP3A4 inhibition. Monitor closely for arrhythmias and other cardiac events. 54. Lonapegsomatropin effects may be decreased by ethinyl estradiol due to reduced serum IGF-1 response. Higher growth hormone doses may be required.
